claim: In response to environments that cause cellular stress, animals engage in sleep behavior that facilitates recovery from the stress.
source: In response to environments that cause cellular stress, animals engage in sleep behavior that facilitates recovery from the stress.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the abstract and introduction sections.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, stress-induced sleep (SIS) is regulated by cytokine activation of the ALA neuron.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, stress-induced sleep(SIS) is regulated by cytokine activation of the ALA neuron, which releases FLP-13 neuropeptides characterized by an amidated arginine-phenylalanine (RFamide) C-terminus motif.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The ALA neuron releases FLP-13 neuropeptides characterized by an amidated arginine-phenylalanine (RFamide) C-terminus motif.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, stress-induced sleep(SIS) is regulated by cytokine activation of the ALA neuron, which releases FLP-13 neuropeptides characterized by an amidated arginine-phenylalanine (RFamide) C-terminus motif.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: dmsr-1 encodes a G-protein coupled receptor similar to an insect RFamide receptor.
source: By performing an unbiased genetic screen for mutants that impair the somnogenic effects of FLP-13 neuropeptides, we identified the gene dmsr-1, which encodes a G-protein coupled receptor similar to an insect RFamide receptor.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic screen results and sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: DMSR-1 is activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell culture.
source: DMSR-1 is activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell culture, is required for SIS in vivo, is expressed non-synaptically in several wake-promoting neurons, and likely couples to a Gi/o heterotrimeric G-protein.
evidence: This is supported by the cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: DMSR-1 is required for SIS in vivo.
source: DMSR-1 is activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell culture, is required for SIS in vivo, is expressed non-synaptically in several wake-promoting neurons, and likely couples to a Gi/o heterotrimeric G-protein.
evidence: This is supported by the genetic experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: DMSR-1 is expressed non-synaptically in several wake-promoting neurons.
source: DMSR-1 is activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell culture, is required for SIS in vivo, is expressed non-synaptically in several wake-promoting neurons, and likely couples to a Gi/o heterotrimeric G-protein.
evidence: This is supported by the expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: DMSR-1 likely couples to a Gi/o heterotrimeric G-protein.
source: DMSR-1 is activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell culture, is required for SIS in vivo, is expressed non-synaptically in several wake-promoting neurons, and likely couples to a Gi/o heterotrimeric G-protein.
evidence: This is inferred from prior studies showing goa-1 mutants are defective in SIS.

claim: During acute infectious illness in mammals, electrophysiological correlates of sleep behavior are observed.
source: During acute infectious illness in mammals, electrophysiological correlates of sleep behavior are observed (Toth and Krueger, 1988, 1989), indicating that the behavioral sequence is sleep.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans, acute illness results in cellular stress, which then induces a sleep behavior.
source: In the arthropod Drosophila melanogaster (Williams et al., 2007; Lenz et al., 2015) and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (Hill et al., 2014), acute illness results in cellular stress, which then induces a sleep behavior: the animals stop moving and feeding, do not respond to weak stimuli but move normally in response to strong stimuli (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stress-induced sleep is beneficial to the animal and helps it recover from the acute injury.
source: This stress-induced sleep (SIS, also known as sickness sleep) is beneficial to the animal and helps it recover from the acute injury (Spiegel et al., 2002; Hill et al., 2014; Kuo and Williams, 2014; Fry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Environments that induce SIS in fruit flies and round worms include bacterial pathogens, bacterial toxins, heat shock, cold shock, osmotic shock, and ultraviolet light exposure.
source: In fruit flies and round worms, environments that induce SIS include bacterial pathogens, bacterial toxins, heat shock, cold shock, osmotic shock, and ultraviolet light exposure (Hill et al., 2014; Lenz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nematode SIS is a distinct sleep state from developmentally timed sleep (DTS).
source: Nematode SIS is a distinct sleep state from a larval sleep state known as developmentally timed sleep (DTS) (Trojanowski et al., 2015), which is regulated by a homolog of the core circadian protein PERIOD (Monsalve et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Developmentally timed sleep is regulated by a homolog of the core circadian protein PERIOD.
source: Nematode SIS is a distinct sleep state from a larval sleep state known as developmentally timed sleep (DTS) (Trojanowski et al., 2015), which is regulated by a homolog of the core circadian protein PERIOD (Monsalve et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the absence of stress, nematodes experience sleep only when they transition between larval stages but do not sleep in the adult stage.
source: In the absence of stress, nematodes experience sleep only when they transition between larval stages but do not sleep in the adult stage.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about C. elegans sleep behavior.

claim: C. elegans does not have an identifiable circadian rhythm of sleep.
source: Since C. elegans does not have an identifiable circadian rhythm of sleep, adult nematodes are an ideal system to study SIS in the absence of the circadian and homeostatic effects of animals that require daily sleep.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about C. elegans.

claim: In mammals, the cytokines interleukin-1 beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha, whose levels increase during an infectious challenge, are each sufficient to induce sleep when injected into the brain.
source: For example, in mammals, the cytokines interleukin-1 beta and tumor necrosis factor alpha, whose levels increase during an infectious challenge, are each sufficient to induce sleep when injected into the brain (reviewed in (Krueger, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In nematodes, arthropods, and mammals, signaling by epidermal growth factor (EGF) is sufficient to induce sleep behavior.
source: In nematodes (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007), arthropods (Foltenyi et al., 2007), and mammals (Kushikata et al., 1998; Kramer et al., 2001), signaling by epidermal growth factor (EGF) is sufficient to induce sleep behavior and, at least in nematodes, EGF signaling is necessary for SIS (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In nematodes, EGF signaling is necessary for SIS.
source: In nematodes (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007), arthropods (Foltenyi et al., 2007), and mammals (Kushikata et al., 1998; Kramer et al., 2001), signaling by epidermal growth factor (EGF) is sufficient to induce sleep behavior and, at least in nematodes, EGF signaling is necessary for SIS (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In mammals, CNS neurons that regulate sleep reside in the hypothalamus.
source: In mammals, CNS neurons that regulate sleep reside in the hypothalamus (Saper et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In C. elegans, the target for EGF action is a single interneuron called ALA.
source: In C. elegans, the target for EGF action is a single interneuron called ALA (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007), whose developmental program has similarities to the developmental program of mammalian neuroendocrine cells (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The developmental program of ALA has similarities to the developmental program of mammalian neuroendocrine cells.
source: In C. elegans, the target for EGF action is a single interneuron called ALA (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007), whose developmental program has similarities to the developmental program of mammalian neuroendocrine cells (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: With EGF activation, ALA depolarizes to release neuropeptides encoded by the gene flp-13 to promote sleep.
source: With EGF activation, ALA depolarizes to release neuropeptides encoded by the gene flp-13 (FMRFamide-Like Peptide-13) to promote sleep (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FLP-13 peptides are characterized by an amidated Arginine-Phenylalanine (RFamide) motif at their C-termini.
source: FLP-13 peptides are characterized by an amidated Arginine-Phenylalanine (RFamide) motif at their C-termini.
evidence: This is based on the peptide sequences shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RFamide neuropeptides are involved in many physiological functions in both invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: RFamide neuropeptides are involved in many physiological functions in both invertebrates (López-Vera et al., 2008; Peymen et al., 2014), and vertebrates (Rőszer and Bánfalvi, 2012; Kim, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In fruit flies, several RFamide neuropeptides regulate sleep.
source: In fruit flies, several RFamide neuropeptides regulate sleep (He et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2013), including the RFamide neuropeptide FMRFamide, which regulates SIS (Lenz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The RFamide neuropeptide FMRFamide regulates SIS in fruit flies.
source: In fruit flies, several RFamide neuropeptides regulate sleep (He et al., 2013; Shang et al., 2013), including the RFamide neuropeptide FMRFamide, which regulates SIS (Lenz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Both locomotion quiescence and feeding quiescence induced by flp-13 can be reversed by activation of motor neurons.
source: Both locomotion quiescence and feeding quiescence induced by flp-13 can be reversed by activation of motor neurons (Trojanowski et al., 2015), suggesting that flp-13 mediates quiescence at the level of the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: flp-13 mediates quiescence at the level of the nervous system.
source: Both locomotion quiescence and feeding quiescence induced by flp-13 can be reversed by activation of motor neurons (Trojanowski et al., 2015), suggesting that flp-13 mediates quiescence at the level of the nervous system.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that motor neuron activation reverses flp-13 induced quiescence.

claim: Quiescence induced by flp-13 requires the G protein alpha subunit GOA-1.
source: Furthermore, quiescence induced by flp-13 requires the G protein alpha subunit GOA-1 (Trojanowski et al., 2015), suggesting that these peptides signal through a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FLP-13 peptides signal through a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
source: Furthermore, quiescence induced by flp-13 requires the G protein alpha subunit GOA-1 (Trojanowski et al., 2015), suggesting that these peptides signal through a G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR).
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for GOA-1.

claim: There are more than 150 genes in the C. elegans genome predicted to encode neuropeptide receptor GPCRs.
source: There are more than 150 genes in the C. elegans genome predicted to encode neuropeptide receptor GPCRs (Frooninckx et al., 2012; Hobert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FRPR-4 can be activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell-based assay.
source: In prior detailed analysis of one of these GPCRs (Nelson et al., 2015), we showed that while FRPR-4 can be activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell-based assay, its genetic removal does not abrogate flp-13 induced quiescence in vivo, suggesting that it is not the receptor mediating the quiescence-inducing effects of FLP-13 peptides in response to cellular stress.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Genetic removal of FRPR-4 does not abrogate flp-13 induced quiescence in vivo.
source: In prior detailed analysis of one of these GPCRs (Nelson et al., 2015), we showed that while FRPR-4 can be activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell-based assay, its genetic removal does not abrogate flp-13 induced quiescence in vivo, suggesting that it is not the receptor mediating the quiescence-inducing effects of FLP-13 peptides in response to cellular stress.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: FRPR-4 is not the receptor mediating the quiescence-inducing effects of FLP-13 peptides in response to cellular stress.
source: In prior detailed analysis of one of these GPCRs (Nelson et al., 2015), we showed that while FRPR-4 can be activated by FLP-13 peptides in cell-based assay, its genetic removal does not abrogate flp-13 induced quiescence in vivo, suggesting that it is not the receptor mediating the quiescence-inducing effects of FLP-13 peptides in response to cellular stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that FRPR-4 removal does not affect flp-13 induced quiescence.

claim: Phsp-16.2:flp-13 transgenic animals are quiescent for body and pharyngeal movements two hours after exposure to a heat pulse to induce flp-13 gene expression.
source: Phsp-16.2:flp-13 transgenic animals are quiescent for body and pharyngeal movements two hours after exposure to a heat pulse to induce flp-13 gene expression (Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: Five identified mutants (qn45, qn49, qn51, qn52 and qn53) are alleles of the same gene.
source: By performing genetic complementation tests, we determined that five of the identified mutants (qn45, qn49, qn51, qn52 and qn53) were alleles of the same gene (Yuan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by genetic complementation tests.

claim: Each of the six mutants had a mutation in dmsr-1, a gene predicted to encode a GPCR.
source: To identify the gene mutated to cause the defect in flp-13 induced quiescence, we sequenced the genomes of six of the allelic mutants. Each of the six mutants had a mutation in dmsr-1, a gene predicted to encode a GPCR (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Four of the mutants (qn44, qn49, qn51 and qn53) contained premature stop codons.
source: Four of the mutants (qn44, qn49, qn51 and qn53) contained premature stop codons.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One mutant (qn45) contained a complex rearrangement in exon 4 consisting of deletion of 332 nucleotides coupled with insertion of 54 nucleotides.
source: One mutant (qn45) contained a complex rearrangement in exon 4 consisting of deletion of 332 nucleotides coupled with insertion of 54 nucleotides (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The qn45 rearrangement results in a frame shift that eliminates the three transmembrane domains at the C-terminus of the protein.
source: This rearrangement results in a frame shift that eliminates the three transmembrane domains at the C-terminus of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: One mutant (qn52) contained an alanine to valine mutation in exon 3.
source: One mutant (qn52) contained an alanine to valine mutation in exon 3.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMSR-1 is one of 41 C. elegans proteins in the RFamide receptor family.
source: DMSR-1 is one of 41 C. elegans proteins in the RFamide receptor family (Frooninckx et al., 2012) and is orthologous to Drosophila receptors for the neuropeptides dromyosuppressin and FMRFamide.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DMSR-1 is orthologous to Drosophila receptors for the neuropeptides dromyosuppressin and FMRFamide.
source: DMSR-1 is one of 41 C. elegans proteins in the RFamide receptor family (Frooninckx et al., 2012) and is orthologous to Drosophila receptors for the neuropeptides dromyosuppressin and FMRFamide.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dromyosuppressin and FMRFamide are neuropeptides with an amidated Arginine-Phenylalanine (RFamide) motif at their C-terminus.
source: Like FLP-13 peptides, Dromyosuppressin and FMRFamide are neuropeptides with an amidated Arginine-Phenylalanine (RFamide) motif at their C-terminus (Nachman et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: All wild-type animals pumped their pharynxes rapidly two hours after the heat pulse whereas the Phsp-16.2:flp-13 transgenic animals showed little to no feeding movements.
source: All wild-type animals pumped their pharynxes rapidly two hours after the heat pulse whereas the Phsp-16.2:flp-13 transgenic animals showed little to no feeding movements (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: A significant fraction of each of the dmsr-1 mutants had pharyngeal pumping movements despite overexpression of flp-13.
source: By contrast, a significant fraction of each of the dmsr-1 mutants had pharyngeal pumping movements despite overexpression of flp-13 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of a heat pulse, dmsr-1(qn45) mutants pumped rapidly at a rate no different from wild-type animals.
source: In the absence of a heat pulse, dmsr-1(qn45) mutants pumped rapidly at a rate no different from wild-type animals (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following induction of flp-13 overexpression, the rate of pumping in dmsr-1(qn45) mutants was not changed.
source: Following induction of flp-13 overexpression, the rate of pumping in dmsr-1(qn45) mutants was not changed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following induction of flp-13 overexpression, dmsr-1(qn45) mutants had increased body movement activity and reduced body movement quiescence in comparison to animals that were wild type for dmsr-1.
source: Following induction of flp-13 overexpression, dmsr-1(qn45) mutants had increased body movement activity and reduced body movement quiescence in comparison to animals that were wild type for dmsr-1 (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: dmsr-1 mutants showed wild-type levels of feeding quiescence in response to EGF overexpression.
source: While dmsr-1 mutants showed wild-type levels of feeding quiescence in response to EGF overexpression (Figure 3A), they had a small but highly significant defect relative to wild-type worms in body movement quiescence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: dmsr-1 mutants had a small but highly significant defect relative to wild-type worms in body movement quiescence in response to EGF overexpression.
source: While dmsr-1 mutants showed wild-type levels of feeding quiescence in response to EGF overexpression (Figure 3A), they had a small but highly significant defect relative to wild-type worms in body movement quiescence (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: dmsr-1 is required downstream of or in parallel to EGF.
source: This result provides evidence that dmsr-1 is required downstream of or in parallel to EGF.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dmsr-1 mutants have defects in EGF-induced quiescence.

claim: There are other ALA-regulated signaling pathways working in parallel to dmsr-1.
source: The observation of only partial suppression of the EGF-induced quiescence suggests that there are other ALA-regulated signaling pathways working in parallel to dmsr-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial suppression of EGF-induced quiescence by dmsr-1 mutations.

claim: dmsr-1 mutations suppressed SIS with respect to both body movement quiescence and feeding quiescence.
source: To test the hypothesis that dmsr-1 mediates SIS, we induced sleep by exposing the animals to a heat stress of 35°C for 30 min. dmsr-1 mutations suppressed SIS with respect to both body movement quiescence and feeding quiescence (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The dmsr-1(qn45) mutation suppressed SIS at temperatures ranging from 34 to 37 degrees.
source: To test whether dmsr-1 was required for SIS after exposure to other temperatures, we exposed cohorts of animals to temperatures ranging from 29 to 37 degrees Celsius. The dmsr-1(qn45) mutation suppressed SIS at temperatures ranging from 34 to 37 degrees (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UVC induced a strong body movement quiescent response, which was attenuated in the dmsr-1(qn45) mutant.
source: To test whether dmsr-1 was required for sleep in response to stressors other than heat, we exposed animals to ultraviolet C (UVC) radiation. UVC induced a strong body movement quiescent response, which was attenuated in the dmsr-1(qn45) mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SIS in dmsr-1 mutants was partially restored by expressing a genomic fragment of dmsr-1 including the coding region and 4 kb of upstream regulatory DNA.
source: We partially restored SIS in dmsr-1 mutants by expressing a genomic fragment of dmsr-1 including the coding region and 4 kb of upstream regulatory DNA (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: dmsr-1 mutants had normal quiescence associated with DTS.
source: While dmsr-1 mutants were defective in quiescence associated with SIS, they had normal quiescence associated with DTS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), as previously shown for flp-13 mutants (Nelson et al., 2014), supporting the notion that the DTS and SIS are regulated at least partially differently (Trojanowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: DTS and SIS are regulated at least partially differently.
source: While dmsr-1 mutants were defective in quiescence associated with SIS, they had normal quiescence associated with DTS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D), as previously shown for flp-13 mutants (Nelson et al., 2014), supporting the notion that the DTS and SIS are regulated at least partially differently (Trojanowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of dmsr-1 mutations on SIS versus DTS, and supported by citations.

claim: Each of the seven FLP-13 peptides was capable of activating DMSR-1.
source: Since the FLP-13 protein is processed into seven distinct RFamide peptides (Figure 4B), we performed a dose-response study with each of these seven peptides. Each of these peptides was capable of activating DMSR-1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The most potent activator of DMSR-1 was FLP-13–5, which elicited a 50% maximal response (EC50) at a concentration of 2.3 nM.
source: The most potent activator was FLP-13–5, which elicited a 50% maximal response (EC50) at a concentration of 2.3 nM (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The observed potent activation of DMSR-1 by FLP-13 peptides in this cell based assay supports the hypothesis that DMSR-1 is an in vivo receptor for FLP-13 peptides.
source: The observed potent activation of DMSR-1 by FLP-13 peptides in this cell based assay supports the hypothesis that DMSR-1 is an in vivo receptor for FLP-13 peptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell culture activation data.

claim: The mechanism of feeding and movement quiescence observed with flp-13 overexpression occurs through the inhibition of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: This prediction arises from prior studies indicating that the mechanism of feeding and movement quiescence observed with flp-13 overexpression occurs through the inhibition of cholinergic motor neurons (Trojanowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron.
source: Based on the location of the cell body, the neuronal process morphology, the co-expression of the transgene with other, well-characterized, green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters, and the co-localization of the red fluorescence with green DiO fluorescence, we concluded that dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron (Figure 5C), the paired AIY neurons (Figure 5D), 12 other head neurons, the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail (Figure 5E), and in five other tail neurons.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: dmsr-1 is expressed in the paired AIY neurons.
source: Based on the location of the cell body, the neuronal process morphology, the co-expression of the transgene with other, well-characterized, green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters, and the co-localization of the red fluorescence with green DiO fluorescence, we concluded that dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron (Figure 5C), the paired AIY neurons (Figure 5D), 12 other head neurons, the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail (Figure 5E), and in five other tail neurons.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: dmsr-1 is expressed in 12 other head neurons.
source: Based on the location of the cell body, the neuronal process morphology, the co-expression of the transgene with other, well-characterized, green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters, and the co-localization of the red fluorescence with green DiO fluorescence, we concluded that dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron (Figure 5C), the paired AIY neurons (Figure 5D), 12 other head neurons, the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail (Figure 5E), and in five other tail neurons.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dmsr-1 is expressed in the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail.
source: Based on the location of the cell body, the neuronal process morphology, the co-expression of the transgene with other, well-characterized, green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters, and the co-localization of the red fluorescence with green DiO fluorescence, we concluded that dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron (Figure 5C), the paired AIY neurons (Figure 5D), 12 other head neurons, the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail (Figure 5E), and in five other tail neurons.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: dmsr-1 is expressed in five other tail neurons.
source: Based on the location of the cell body, the neuronal process morphology, the co-expression of the transgene with other, well-characterized, green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporters, and the co-localization of the red fluorescence with green DiO fluorescence, we concluded that dmsr-1 is expressed in the RID neuron (Figure 5C), the paired AIY neurons (Figure 5D), 12 other head neurons, the paired PHA and PHB neurons in the tail (Figure 5E), and in five other tail neurons.
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dmsr-1 is not expressed in AVE or AVA neurons.
source: Importantly, we did not see expression of dmsr-1 in AVE or AVA neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by expression pattern analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: AVE and AVA command interneurons are the only post-synaptic partners to the ALA neuron based on the presence of ultrastructurally-defined chemical synapses.
source: These command interneurons are the only post-synaptic partners to the ALA neuron based on the presence of ultrastructurally-defined chemical synapses (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ALA signals in a neuroendocrine fashion to promote SIS.
source: The expression in neurons that do not make direct synaptic connections with ALA suggested that ALA signals in a neuroendocrine fashion to promote SIS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dmsr-1 is not expressed in ALA's synaptic partners.

claim: A DMSR-1 protein with a GFP fluorescent tag at its C-terminus was localized diffusely to neuronal cell membranes and was not localized to synapses.
source: In support of this suggestion, we found that a DMSR-1 protein with a GFP fluorescent tag at its C-terminus was localized diffusely to neuronal cell membranes and was not localized to synapses (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: GFP-tagged DMSR-1 protein rescued the mutant phenotype of dmsr-1.
source: This GFP-tagged DMSR-1 protein rescued the mutant phenotype of dmsr-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that it was functional.
evidence: This is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ALA can signal via non-synaptic means.
source: The notion that ALA can signal via non-synaptic means was previously proposed based on the observation that a mutant with disrupted ALA axonal outgrowth retained normal ALA function (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Expression of dmsr-1 in the paired PHA tail sensory neurons was not sufficient to restore feeding or body movement quiescence induced by flp-13 overexpression.
source: Expression of dmsr-1 in the paired PHA tail sensory neurons was not sufficient to restore feeding or body movement quiescence induced by flp-13 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Expression of dmsr-1 in the paired head AIY interneurons conferred a small but statistically-significant rescue of the body movement quiescence defect.
source: Expression of dmsr-1 in the paired head AIY interneurons conferred a small but statistically-significant (p<0.01) rescue of the body movement quiescence defect (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D) but not the feeding quiescence defect observed in dmsr-1 mutants during flp-13 overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: AIY specific dmsr-1 expression did not rescue the feeding or body movement quiescence defects observed in dmsr-1 mutants during SIS.
source: AIY specific dmsr-1 expression did not however rescue the feeding or body movement quiescence defects observed in dmsr-1 mutants during SIS (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: When transgenic worms expressing Pdmsr-1:HisCl worms were placed on histamine, their movement quiescence and total activity were not affected.
source: When transgenic worms expressing Pdmsr-1:HisCl worms were placed on histamine, their movement quiescence and total activity were not affected (Figure 6), indicating that in the absence of cellular stress, silencing these neurons has minimal effect on behavior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of cellular stress, silencing dmsr-1 expressing neurons has minimal effect on behavior.
source: When transgenic worms expressing Pdmsr-1:HisCl worms were placed on histamine, their movement quiescence and total activity were not affected (Figure 6), indicating that in the absence of cellular stress, silencing these neurons has minimal effect on behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the HisCl experiment results.

claim: When HisCl worms were placed on histamine following exposure to UV stress, they had reduced total activity and enhanced body movement quiescence compared to control worms that lacked the HisCl channels.

claim: DMSR-1 promotes sleep by inhibiting wake-promoting cells.

evidence: This is inferred from the HisCl experiment results showing enhanced sleep when dmsr-1 expressing neurons are inhibited.

claim: The double mutant animals showed a greater defect in quiescence than either the dmsr-1 or the flp-13 single mutant animals.
source: We compared the SIS phenotypes of flp-13; dmsr-1 double mutant animals to those of dmsr-1 and flp-13 single mutant animals. We reasoned that if flp-13 and dmsr-1 have sleep inducing effects that are independent of one another, then the double mutant will have a greater defect in SIS compared to either of the single mutants. The double mutant animals indeed showed a greater defect in quiescence than either the dmsr-1 or the flp-13 single mutant animals (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.
